NBIS is currently a stock that trades around $115 with a market cap ~$34B. To hit $1,000/share it needs a $280–300B market cap or 8-9× current.

How it could happen:

2026 revenue: ~$3.0–3.2B
2027 guidance: $12–13B (4×) with pre-tax break-even in Q4

Longer term: Successful ramp to multi-GW active capacity by ~2030 could drive revenue to $40 - 60B+ (supported by Microsoft/Meta contracts, >$20 - 25M per MW pricing, and >1 GW/year additions).

At $50B revenue and 5–6× sales, market cap reaches ~$250-300B or 850-1,050/share (assuming limited dilution).

Main supports: Strong customer prepayments funding most new capex, vertical integration, and high AI demand.

Like in any other business there are always some risks : Build delays, funding/dilution from $40B+ annual capex, competition, or demand slowdown.

$1,000 is a multi-year bull-case scenario, not a near-term target. 

Is that possible? Well, there are some folks on X with clearly deep knowledge in the biz calling for a $2,000+ bull scenario.

en_summary: David Friedberg speculates Jensen Huang was 'taken out' because he opposed government control of AI. “I do worry that there is legislation coming our way with the new Congress that is going to say every AI chip and every computer and every data center has a switch and has a connection back to some central system. And that central system will be a state system. And we are fundamentally looking at an Orwellian state explosion if this sort of thing happens. And my guess is that people know Jensen’s philosophy. Jensen has talked a lot about AI being for the benefit of all of humanity, regardless of your country, regardless of your standing, regardless of your wealth. He was anti-oligopoly. He was the opposite of the oligarchy. And the central state, the totalitarian state, represents everything that I believe Jensen was against. And because of that, I think he had to be taken out if ultimately the goal is to have the totalitarian state use this technology as a tool. I really do worry about that being the reason. Because at the end of the day, whoever comes in next has to be cooperative with legislatures and work out a bill that we all agree to, head nodding, standing in front of Congress and saying, ‘You know what? I agree with these new ideas. Let’s all go do this.’ And suddenly the US government has control of the actual physical chips that exist in free markets and exist in data centers around the world. And that’s not a great place for any of us.”

Results indicate improving economics for well-positioned ACA insurers via ~14% planned premium increases, favorable underwriting, competitor withdrawals and admin leverage, but not uniformly improving healthcare. $250M favorable risk adjustment is company-specific. http://www.atlaspeakresearch.com/earnings/oscr/2026-q3/

$OSCR KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM OSCAR HEALTH’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Oscar Health’s results indicate improving economics for well-positioned ACA insurers, not a uniformly improving healthcare environment. The combination of approximately 14% planned premium increases, favorable underwriting experience, competitor withdrawals, and administrative leverage supports selective insurer earnings recovery. Simultaneously, continued eligibility enforcement, coverage interruptions, and tighter medical management create pressure on hospital reimbursement and enrollment economics. The most actionable distinction is between companies retaining more premium through repricing and those absorbing the financial consequences when patients lose coverage. Oscar’s $250 million favorable risk adjustment revision is company-specific and should not be extrapolated across competing insurers. The strongest positive external implications concern Centene’s marketplace recovery, Allstate’s directly identified supplemental-insurance distribution opportunity, and eHealth’s employer-funded individual coverage channel. The strongest negative implications concern hospital payer mix and the continuing cost of verifying and retaining eligible ACA enrollment. Several supporting peer disclosures preceded Oscar’s call; the incremental information is corroboration and improved visibility, not a newly announced earnings event.

text:
They don’t use HBM, but… by their own calculations, running Kimi K3 requires 59 wafers. Leaving that part out and simply saying “we don’t need HBM” is just marketing wordplay.

For now, I see their role as replacing GPUs in certain inference workloads or complementing AMD. AMD GPUs handle prefill, processing the input and long context, while Cerebras handles decode, generating the response quickly.

They understand these limitations too, which is why they’re moving toward 3D stacked DRAM. Eventually, they’ll have to compete for memory supply as well.

Still, I personally think this approach could make sense given the supply chain constraints we’re facing right now. The biggest question is how far they can overcome the technical limitations of wafer scale chips. Whether they can keep operating efficiently as models and systems get larger is something they’ll have to keep proving.

TWO MAJOR NVIDIA SHAREHOLDERS HAVE WRITTEN TO THE BOARD ASKING IT TO LEAVE THE DOOR OPEN FOR JENSEN HUANG'S RETURN

Brad Gerstner, chief executive of Altimeter Capital, and Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer of Atreides Management, have sent a joint letter to $NVDA board.

They ask the board to pursue "a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang."

"There are more questions about recent events than answers," they write, warning the board to "avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders." They say the company will be "capably led in the interim by Colette Kress and team" and that the board has time to get the decision right.

A petition site has also launched demanding the board reinstate Huang pending an independent investigation, under the line "thirty-three years deserve an answer."

Elon Musk has joined the calls for Huang's reinstatement, according to the Washington Post.

The board said earlier today it has not formally engaged any candidates and has not yet selected a search firm.

The long-term lease has not yet been finalized.

Source: FT

AMD $AMD has two major product releases converging at the same time: Venice CPUs and the highly anticipated Helios MI400 Series.

Just three months ago, management expected server CPU revenue to grow more than 70% in 2027, while total Data Center revenue would grow “well over 100%,” driven by the Helios ramp.

Since then, AMD has raised its outlook considerably, and the two product ramps are now exceeding our original expectations.

Server CPU revenue is now expected to more than double in 2027, up from the previous outlook for 70%+ growth. Meanwhile, Data Center AI revenue (GPUs) is expected to significantly more than double.

All-in, AMD guided for companywide revenue to increase more than 80% next year, which is more than twice the company’s long-term growth model outlined at its November 2025 Analyst Day.

Perhaps the most important milestone is that AMD’s Data Center AI business is expected to surpass its server CPU business in revenue for the first time in Q4, as Helios enters a multi-gigawatt cycle with Anthropic, $META, $MSFT, OpenAI, and $ORCL deploying its new racks.

This brings us back to my July 2024 prediction that AMD’s returns would surpass Nvidia $NVDA, a call I made when Nvidia was the market darling.

Since then, AMD has gained more than 250% compared to Nvidia’s 51%, outperforming by about 5X.

And I have a hunch that gap could get wider.

zh_summary: 自2023年以來，現貨鈾價上漲超過50%，長期價格上漲60%。公用事業需求是核心驅動力，不僅是投機。商品不會在供應過剩的市場上漲。回應過去對庫存和Arrow產量的謹慎看法。提及$NXE。
en_summary: Since 2023, spot uranium price up >+50% and LT price up +60%. Utility demand core driver, not just speculation. Commodities don't rise in oversupplied market. Responds to past caution on inventories and Arrow production. Mentions $NXE.
text:
Warren, since 2023 (broadly), the spot uranium price is up > +50% and the LT price is up +60%. While some financial speculation has aided this move, utility demand has been the core driver. I know I don't have to tell you this, but commodities don't rise in price in an oversupplied market.

In Sept. 2023, you mentioned the enormous commercial inventories and the 30mil lbs/yr from Arrow that would "flood the market in a few years" as reasons for caution. The four months that followed that post, the spot price doubled and the equities tripled. And while there was again some speculators involved in that move, everyone was buying following two large RFPs that year (PG&E in Q2, KHNP in Q3) – utilities, traders, funds, and producers (Cameco, THK (KAP), UG (Orano), etc.).

I have been wrong countless times with short-term expectations, so I'm not trying to take my own victory lap regarding the commodity's trajectory. But to claim you were right about a lacking supply deficit when the information regarding the commodity's price move over the past 3 years is there for all to see – simply because the equities are getting thrashed due to AI/Vol basket correlation – is a poor take. 

I'd suggest looking at the forward curve for the commodity, including the long-term contract terms currently being signed. That's a better way to gauge where price is headed than looking at strategic commercial inventories that are not and will not be for sale, or at developers' investor presentations.

Financing:
The 2027 outlook assumes $17–20bn of customer prepayments, and a significant part of that is committed under existing contracts and paid before the capacity is delivered.

Management sees third-party colocation partners as less reliable, sometimes one to two months late or more, which is why most 2027 data centers will be company-owned.
